source.title: Verifying the Linear Representation Hypothesis: How Interpretable Are Vision SAEs?
source.authors: Teodor Chiaburu; Franz Motzkus; Frank Haußer; F. Biessmann

record.file_problem: none noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends automated neuron-explanation scoring to vision SAE features and image patches, using a caption-based AIS procedure and reporting results.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates explanations generated from highly activating examples by simulating activations on other high-activating and random image patches. The main AIS results bear on V6. It does not report the share of language-model neurons meeting a defined good-score threshold, as V7 specifies. Cited findings from other studies and non-AIS table metrics are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study adapts Bills et al.'s simulation-based AIS, one of the original sources, to score vision SAE features, not a model's own neurons, on captioned image patches. It uses the scoring method as an evaluation tool. Its results describe a related but different construct, the interpretability of trained SAE dictionary features in vision encoders. None of the versions names this: V6 and V7 concern neuron explanations, and V7 specifically concerns new text. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the results as challenging the Linear Representation Hypothesis underlying SAEs. They report that vision SAE features remain rather opaque (AIS and MS all below 0.5) despite high reconstruction R2. They describe their caption-based AIS as comparable to NLP baselines and aligned with human judgment (r=0.62 on 14 survey images).
record.recipe_differences: Adapts AIS to vision SAE features by captioning image patches, explaining from five high-activation images, and simulating activations on five other high-activation images plus five random images. It computes Pearson correlation on patch activations; the original method was for sequence-model features.
record.method_sensitivity: AIS varied by SAE architecture, embedder, dataset, and explainer/simulator Gemma model. The paper also reports layer-dependent AIS in Table 5, but those results are not catalogued here.

fits_no_version.finding: Caption-based simulation AIS of vision SAE features is low across 27 SAE/embedder/dataset configurations. Mean AIS ranges 0.02–0.43, with TopK SAEs lowest. Per-feature p<0.05 rates are 36–81% (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations of vision SAE features built from top-activating patches predict held-out patch activations only weakly (mean AIS < 0.5), varying by SAE architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The No-SAE condition on DINO/CUB scores raw embedding dimensions with AIS 0.24–0.30 across layers. This is lower than the Vanilla SAE at most layers, but MS is higher (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a vision transformer, raw embedding dimensions are only weakly predictable from activating-example explanations under simulation scoring.

record.problems: AIS depends on caption quality, caption grid resolution, and explainer/simulator performance, so low AIS cannot be attributed solely to SAE feature interpretability. The user study had 16 valid users and surveyed only two selected features. AIS simulation uses a comparatively small set of held-out images per feature.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's other metrics (sparsity, reconstruction R2, OOD score, coherence, connectivity, and MS) are not AIS or tests of the V6 behavior. Table 4 repeats Table 2's AIS values with medians and significance rates, so those repeated results are not duplicated. Table 5's layer-wise and raw-embedding AIS results are omitted because the flattened table does not clearly identify the layer for its first row.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares.
No neuron-pole shares across language models or scales.
No analysis of InceptionV1 cat-and-car or other canonical polysemantic neurons.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron share versus tools or architecture; SAE architecture comparisons concern dictionary features, not neurons.
No attribution graphs from native neurons.
Explanations are scored on SAE features, not native neurons. The only native-unit result is raw DINO embedding dimensions (Table 5), which are residual coordinates, not neurons.
No simulation scoring of language-model neuron explanations on new text. Per-feature significance rates (Table 4) are for vision SAE features.

missing.what: No-SAE AIS for raw DINO embedding dimensions: 0.2764 final layer, 0.2376 layer 8, 0.2768 layer 5, 0.2971 layer 2, with many NaNs. These are the only native-unit results and would matter if raw embedding dimensions were counted as neurons for V6/V7.
missing.versions: V6, V7 (only if residual coordinates are accepted as neurons)

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6 and gave a 'supports' label. That is withdrawn: SAE dictionary features are a trained replacement basis, not the model's own neurons. This is precisely the distinction V5 draws, and the essay's claims concern native neurons. The T1 and T3 rows validate or ablate the study's own method. The study is not an original source. No labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report the shares with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Does not test whether the claimed neuron-pole shares hold across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
Does not investigate InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons in InceptionV1-sized models or test whether that share rises with tools or architecture.
Does not build attribution graphs from a large model's own neurons or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model.
Tests vision SAE features on image-patch captions, not native language-model neurons on text; it does not quantify the prevalence of this failure in the Qwen3-32B audit.
Reports vision SAE AIS values and per-neuron significance rates, but not the proportion of language-model neurons attaining a defined good-score threshold on new text.
